stories.title: Three, including child, killed in strikes on Kyiv region
stories.summary: Russian strikes has killed three people, including a child, in a district northeast of Ukraine's capital, a regional military official said, as Kyiv warned of incoming ballistic missiles. Moscow has significantly upped its attacks on the Ukrainian capital in recent months, typically firing salvos of hard-to-intercept ballistic missiles in short blitzes that rock buildings and send booms echoing across the city. On a post on Telegram, head of the regional military administration Tymur Tkachenko said three people, including a child, were killed and three others were wounded in strikes in Brovary district northeast of Kyiv. Falling debris from the attacks damaged houses and vehicles and caused a fire in a non-residential building, he said.

stories.title: HIQA: Concerns found during centre's inspection rectified
stories.summary: An inspection of a Tusla operated children's residential centre in June by the Health Information and Quality Authority (HIQA) found that safety concerns highlighted during a previous inspection had been rectified. In February, HIQA found that the centre was not compliant with all five national standards assessed. There were immediate risks to the safety, health and welfare of the three children living in the centre at that time, which included the use of illicit substances. In June, HIQA found that of the five national standards, the centre was compliant with one and substantially compliant with the remaining four standards.

stories.title: Government insists new jet can land in bad weather
stories.summary: The Coalition has insisted there are no issues with a new Government jet after reports it may struggle to land in bad weather. It has been suggested the new aircraft may not be able to land in foggy weather as it was ordered without key navigation equipment from an Israeli firm. The Government adopted a policy in 2024 of not awarding Israeli companies defence contracts owing to an advisory opinion from the International Court of Justice against Israeli settlements in the West Bank. The Journal.ie reported how the €53 million aircraft was purchased from a French firm without a FalconEye system, which normally sits on the plane's nose and helps it land in fog or other weather conditions that limit visibility, as it was made by an Israeli manufacturer.

stories.title: Kingspan raises profit forecast on data centre demand
stories.summary: Shares in insulation and building materials group Kingspan jumped almost 20% in Dublin trade today after it raised its full-year profit guidance. Kingspan said it was raising its guidance due to its data centre construction operations that it says are benefiting from a burgeoning tech sector which is detached from the regular economy. Co Cavan-based Kingspan expects full-year trading profit to jump by about 18% to €1.13 billion, up from a forecast of €1.05 billion in late April. The company said it can also reasonably expect to break through €10 billion in annual revenue for the first time.

stories.title: Europe readies for solar eclipse dip in power generation
stories.summary: European energy operators are braced for next week's solar eclipse to cause a temporary dip in power generation and have taken steps to keep electricity flowing to businesses and consumers, an industry body has said. While the 12 August eclipse offers a rare spectacle for the general public, it presents a technical challenge for grid operators, which must constantly balance electricity supply and demand to guarantee secure power provision. "Under clear-sky conditions, photovoltaic (PV) output could decrease by up to 9.7 GW across Europe, creating a rapid but predictable change in generation patterns between 7.15pm and 9.30pm CEST," said the association representing Europe's power grid operators, ENTSO-E. It said operators were "ready to ensure the secure and stable operation of the electricity system throughout the event".

stories.title: Hoops' wild defeat of Dundalk marred by fan confrontation
stories.summary: Shamrock Rovers stretched their lead at the top of the SSE Airtricity Men's Premier Division to 10 points after a wild first half that yielded all five goals and saw a geed-up home fan confront Dundalk players on the pitch. By full-time, referee Rob Harvey had dished out 11 yellow cards - including to both managers - having also shown Rovers coach Sean Kavanagh a red in the tunnel at half-time. It was an all-or-nothing sort of night in Tallaght, and you couldn't take your eyes off it. Dundalk were the only team Rovers hadn’t beaten this season but the Hoops’ first-half display was littered with so many mistakes, it’s a wonder how they led on three occasions through Dylan Watts, Michael Noonan and Jonathan Afolabi.

stories.title: Cork's Kabia becomes Leyton Orient's record signing
stories.summary: Cork forward Jaze Kabia has joined English League One side Leyton Orient in what is a record transfer fee for the Os. Kabia joins from Grimsby Town on a three-year deal for an undisclosed fee, but revealed by the club to be the biggest they've ever paid for a player. Kabia joins on the back of a superb finish to last season with Grimsby, with the player scoring 24 goals in 57 appearances for the League Two side in 2025/26. Previously with Cobh Ramblers, Shelbourne and Cork City, he scored in the penalty shoot-out last season as Grimsby shocked Manchester United in the Carabao Cup.

stories.title: Unexpected job losses in US last month
stories.summary: The US economy unexpectedly shed jobs in July and nonfarm payrolls for the previous month were revised sharply lower, potentially raising questions about whether the Federal Reserve will increase interest rates next month. Nonfarm payrolls decreased by 23,000 jobs last month after a downwardly revised 20,000 increase in June, the Labor Department's Bureau of Labor Statistics said in its closely watched employment report today. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast payrolls rising 80,000 after advancing by a previously reported 57,000 in June. Estimates ranged from as low as 10,000 to as high as 140,000 jobs added. Payrolls, however, have a tendency to be softer in July. Economists have viewed the labour market as being in a "slow hire, slow fire" mode.

stories.title: Derry ease past Sligo but McClean future looks uncertain
stories.summary: Derry City ended a topsy-turvy week with a comfortable SSE Airtricity Men's Premier Division victory over bottom side Sligo Rovers at the Ryan McBride Brandywell Stadium. With manager Tiernan Lynch and his assistant, and brother, Seamus both leaving the club by mutual consent and replaced by the club's director of football Mark Connolly on an interim basis, the Foylesiders secured the points thanks to second-half goals from Barry Cotter and Adam O'Reilly. Ex-Republic of Ireland international James McClean's future with his home town club looks to be in doubt. Before kick-off, he posted a picture on social media that suggested he was at home watching his former club Wrexham take on Middlesbrough in the Carabao Cup on TV. McClean had on a number of occasions criticised Derry during Lynch's reign and his absence tonight may cast doubt over his long-term future.

stories.title: The extraordinary life and times of Kerry music mogul Bill Fuller
stories.summary: Analysis: A new film tells the little-known story of the pioneering venue owner and colourful music promoter whose business empire spanned the globe Here's a question to consider - and it says a lot about national values. When Irish people go out for the night: (i) should they dance domestic dances under the close supervision of priests and holy men or (ii) should they be allowed to dance to well-known local and international names in venues operated as businesses? If you chose option (ii) you might have Bill Fuller to thank. And, like most Irish people, you’ve probably never heard his name. When Ireland achieved independence, politicians turned their attention to what it meant to be Irish. How could Ireland keep its traditional values in a rapidly changing world? A large part of this national public discussion focused on the threat from abroad. The Catholic hierarchy wanted to safeguard the country from anything that could undermine the moral order. The Church was very worried about communism, 'immoral’ films and rock ‘n’ roll. But one of the biggest challenges to the Catholic hierarchy didn't come from Moscow or Memphis but from the mountains of Co Kerry. When the Catholic hierarchy and members of the Irish judiciary were preaching against the 'evils' of jazz music, Fuller was bringing prominent jazz musicians and rock 'n’ roll acts, including Stan Kenton, to perform in Ireland.

stories.title: Armagh Observatory to host special event for solar eclipse
stories.summary: On Wednesday, 12 August, the moon will cover approximately 94% of the sun, causing a partial solar eclipse. It will be the deepest eclipse seen from the UK and Ireland since the total eclipse of August 1999, and the last time that such an eclipse will be seen here until 2090. A total solar eclipse will cover a narrow path of our planet, likely crossing Greenland, Iceland, northern Spain, and a small portion of Portugal. Although Ireland won't see a total eclipse, the 94% partial eclipse has been eagerly awaited by professionals in the field for decades.

It also details how the patient will be monitored, practical standards like water temperature and depth, and emergency procedures.

stories.title: Tensions cool between EU and Spain over crisis in Ceuta
stories.summary: The Government will likely breathe a sigh of relief as the political temperature surrounding Spain's handling of the migrant crisis in Ceuta cools after some fractious exchanges among EU member states in recent days. Minister for Justice Jim O'Callaghan was forced to convene an emergency meeting of EU interior and justice ministers after the images of over 50,000 people swimming across the border from Morocco to the Spanish North African territory pushed immigration to the top of the agenda for Ireland's EU Presidency. This morning's meeting came with Spain on the offensive - expressing annoyance at the lack of solidarity from other EU members and accusing some of turning the crisis into an attack on its Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez. Others wanted swift action against Madrid - with Italy and Denmark last week advocating for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen free-travel area over the crisis; 20 other countries joined them in saying the EU should continue pressing their tough line on immigration, seemingly at odds with Spain's open stance on migration.

stories.title: FBD's H1 profit before tax more than doubles to €43m
stories.summary: Insurance group FBD Holdings has reported higher profits for the first six months of the year and said it remains focused on maintaining its momentum for the second half of 2026. FBD said its half year insurance revenue rose by 7.6% to €253.1m compared to €235.1m the same time last year. Gross written premium - the largest part of insurance revenue - was 3.8% higher at €258.4m from €248.9m the same time last year with growth across Farmer, Retail and direct Business sectors. FBD said its overall average premiums increased by 3.4% compared to the same time last year, comprising a 2.5% increase relating to increased liability and property coverage.

stories.title: UEFA boycott remains despite FIFA private sale retraction
stories.summary: UEFA still plans to boycott all FIFA-related events despite FIFA president Gianni Infantino issuing an apology and retracting the plans for selling ownership shares in the World Cup. UEFA's 55 member federations unanimously approved the FIFA boycott at an emergency meeting on July 30 after Infantino announced a plan to raise billions in private equity under a new entity called the FIFA Forward Enterprise. UEFA's response reportedly played a large role in this plan being shelved. However, the reversal hasn't immediately convinced UEFA to buy back into FIFA under Infantino. "UEFA's associations were very clear about the conditions attached to the non participation in FIFA competitions," UEFA said in a statement.

stories.title: Galway boss Murray not interested in trilogy decider talk
stories.summary: Galway manager Cathal Murray doesn't view Sunday’s All-Ireland Camogie final against Cork as any sort of trilogy decider. While the two counties sit far apart on the roll of honour – Cork out in front with 30 titles and Galway joint-sixth with Tipperary on five – it is undoubtedly the key rivalry in the game right now. That has been evident over recent seasons as Croke Park prepares for a third straight final between the two counties – the first time the pair have managed that since meeting three times from 1996 to '98. On that occasion, Galway won the first All-Ireland, Cork the second with the Rebels retaining in 1998.
